what: BlackBerry no longer makes phones. It sells software: QNX, an operating system embedded in car electronics that controls safety-critical systems, and cybersecurity products for governments and businesses, including secure communications.
customers: Carmakers and their electronics suppliers embedding QNX in vehicles, and government agencies and enterprises buying secure communications and endpoint security.
money: Embedded operating system royalties from carmakers and industrial customers.
Secure communications and endpoint security for governments and enterprises.
moat: QNX is the valuable asset: it is certified to the automotive safety standards required for systems where a software failure could kill someone, and that certification takes years. Once a carmaker builds a vehicle platform on QNX, it stays for the platform's life and the next generation too, because requalifying an operating system is enormously expensive.
risks: Revenue has been erratic and declining — $718.0M in 2022, $534.9M in 2025, $549.1M in 2026 — after years of restructuring and divestitures.
The shares trade at about 64.6 times earnings, 8.0 times sales and 48.0 times EV/EBITDA, which is a very high price for a business this size and this flat.
The cybersecurity business competes against CrowdStrike and Palo Alto, which are vastly larger and growing fast.
QNX royalties depend on car production volumes, which have been weak.
Seven analysts average a $9.80 target, about 17% above the current price.
opportunities: QNX is certified to automotive safety standards, which takes years and keeps competitors out of safety-critical systems.
Once a vehicle platform is built on QNX, it stays for the platform's life and usually the next one, which makes the revenue visible.
Cash of $359.9M against $224.8M of debt is a net cash position.
Software content per vehicle is rising sharply as cars become computers, which raises QNX royalties per car over time.
Free cash flow of $92.1M on $614.0M of revenue shows the business now generates cash.
watch: QNX royalty revenue and design wins, separately from cybersecurity. QNX is the asset; the rest is history.
view: BlackBerry is now essentially one asset with a cybersecurity business attached, and the honest way to analyse it is to value QNX and treat the rest as optionality. QNX is an operating system embedded in car electronics, certified to the automotive safety standards required where a software failure could kill someone. That certification takes years to obtain, and once a carmaker builds a vehicle platform on it, QNX stays for that platform's life and usually the next generation too, because requalifying an operating system across a safety-critical system is enormously expensive.

The structural tailwind for QNX is real: cars are becoming computers, software content per vehicle is rising sharply, and the number of electronic control units running certified software grows with every model generation. Royalties per car should rise over time independently of how many cars get built. That is a genuine long-duration asset.

The cybersecurity business is the part I would discount heavily. It competes against CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks, both vastly larger, faster-growing and better capitalised. BlackBerry's strength there is government and secure communications, which is a real niche, but it is not a business that grows into something large from here.

What makes the stock hard is the price. Revenue has been erratic and declining — $718 million in 2022 down to $549 million in 2026 — after years of restructuring, and the shares trade at 64.6 times earnings and 8 times sales. For a company this size with flat revenue, that multiple is paying for QNX's future rather than the present business. The net cash position of $360 million against $225 million of debt removes financing risk, which helps. QNX royalty revenue and design wins are the only numbers worth tracking; everything else here is legacy.
bull: Rising software content per vehicle lifts QNX royalties on a certification moat that keeps competitors out of safety-critical automotive systems.
bear: Car production stays weak, the cybersecurity business keeps losing to far larger rivals, and a 64 times earnings multiple on declining revenue corrects.
